blocks.text: I can {compare and order} decimal numbers with hundredths.
In this lesson you will decide which decimal number is larger, and put a list of decimals in order.

items.title: compare numbers with the {same whole number}

blocks.text: Tap each word to see what it means.

items.def: When you compare, you look for similarities and differences in an object or value.
The value of a digit in a number based on where it is placed.
Putting numbers or objects in position based on a set rule.
When items are arranged from smallest to largest.
When items are arranged from largest to smallest.

blocks.text: One big block is one whole. One flat block is one tenth. One little block is one hundredth.
Izzy has 1 whole, 4 tenths and 3 hundredths. That is **1.43**.
Alex has 2 wholes, 3 tenths and 4 hundredths. That is **2.34**.

blocks.label: Who has the larger number?
blocks.text: **Alex.** Not because of the number of blocks, but because he has more ones: 2 wholes is more than 1 whole.
We use symbols to compare numbers. The symbol opens towards the larger number.
On a number line, larger numbers are further to the {right}.

slides.title: Start with the largest place value

blocks.text: Put both numbers in a place value chart. Then follow this rule:
To compare two numbers, compare the digits with the {same place value}, starting with the {largest} place value.
1.43 and 2.34: the largest place value here is the **ones**. 2 ones is more than 1 one, so 2.34 is larger.
Order 23.47, 7.68 and 2.3 from smallest to largest (ascending).

items: Largest place value: 23.47 has 2 **tens**. The others have none, so 23.47 is the largest.
Next look at the ones: 7.68 has 7 ones and 2.3 has 2 ones, so 7.68 is bigger than 2.3.

blocks.label: Watch out!
blocks.text: 2.3 has fewer digits than 7.68 or 23.47, but that does not decide anything. What matters is the place value of each digit, starting with the largest.

slides.title: Quick check: the largest place value

blocks.why: 5.01 has 5 ones and 4.58 only has 4 ones. Compare the ones first.
10.2 has a 1 in the tens column. The other two numbers have no tens.
All three have 3 ones. Then compare tenths: 3.09 has 0 tenths, the smallest.

blocks.text: Now compare 3.41 and 3.14. What do you notice?
They have the same number of ones (3). When the ones are the same, we compare the next largest place value: the **tenths**.
4 tenths is greater than 1 tenth, so **3.41 > 3.14**.
Similarly, 0.1 and 0.01 have the same number of ones (0). 0.1 has 1 tenth and 0.01 has none, so 0.1 is larger.
Now compare 3.41 and 3.43. Same ones, and the same tenths (4).
When the tenths are the same, we compare the next largest place value: the **hundredths**.
1 hundredth is less than 3 hundredths, so **3.41 < 3.43**.

blocks.label: Another way with 7.67 and 7.68
blocks.text: When the whole numbers are the same you can read the tenths and hundredths together as hundredths: 7 and 67 hundredths, 7 and 68 hundredths. 68 hundredths is larger, so 7.68 is the larger number.
Which is larger, 1.5 or 1.45?
You can convert the tenths into hundredths to compare.

rows.note: 5 tenths can also be written as 50 hundredths.

blocks.text: 50 hundredths is greater than 45 hundredths, so **1.5 > 1.45**.

blocks.label: Watch out!
blocks.text: Having more digits does not make a number larger. 1.5 has fewer digits than 1.45 but it is the larger number. In the same way, 2 is larger than 1.45 because 2 ones is more than 1 one.

blocks.q: Choose <, > or = to complete each comparison.
Tap a number, then tap the column it belongs in.

blocks.text: These numbers look very similar: 1.40, 4.1, 4.01, 1.04. Order them from largest to smallest (descending).

items: Ones: 4.1 and 4.01 have 4 ones. 1.40 and 1.04 have 1 one. So the 4s come first.
4.1 and 4.01: tenths 1 and 0, so 4.1 is larger.
1.40 and 1.04: tenths 4 and 0, so 1.40 is larger.

blocks.q: Put 0.5, 0.05, 0.55 and 0.15 in ascending order (smallest to largest). Which list is correct?
blocks.why: Compare tenths first: 0.05 has 0 tenths, 0.15 has 1, 0.5 has 5 and 0.55 has 5. The last two are equal in tenths, so compare hundredths: 0.5 < 0.55.

blocks.q: Put 6.08, 6.8, 0.68 and 8.06 in descending order (largest to smallest). Which list is correct?
blocks.why: Ones first: 8, 6, 6, 0. Then 6.8 has 8 tenths and 6.08 has 0 tenths, so 6.8 > 6.08.

items: To compare two numbers, compare the digits with the same place value, starting with the largest place value.
If the digits are the same, look at the next largest place value.
You can compare tenths and hundredths by converting the tenths into hundredths.
If you can compare numbers, you can order them: ascending (smallest to largest) or descending (largest to smallest).

blocks.text: More digits does not mean a larger number. Always start with the {largest place value}.

flashcards.back: The value of a digit in a number based on where it is placed.

flashcards.front: Where do you start when you compare two numbers?
flashcards.back: With the digits of the largest place value.

flashcards.front: Two numbers have the same ones. What do you compare next?
Two numbers have the same ones and the same tenths. What do you compare next?
Where are larger numbers on a number line?

flashcards.back: 3.41. The ones are the same, and 4 tenths is more than 1 tenth.

flashcards.front: Is 1.5 or 1.45 larger? How can you tell?
flashcards.back: 1.5. Write 1.5 as 1.50: 50 hundredths is more than 45 hundredths.

flashcards.front: Does a number with more digits always have a greater value?
flashcards.back: No. 1.5 is larger than 1.45, and 2 is larger than 1.45.

worksheet.title: Worksheet: Compare and order decimal numbers with hundredths
worksheet.instructions: For the comparison questions, write <, > or = in the gap. Start by comparing the largest place value each time. For the ordering questions, write the numbers in a row, separated by commas.

questions.explanation: 0.81 has 0 ones and 1.32 has 1 one, so 0.81 is less than 1.32.
1 one is less than 2 ones, so 1.26 < 2.06.
Both have 2 tens, but 3 ones is more than 2 ones, so 23.10 > 22.10.
The tens, ones and tenths are the same. 4 hundredths is less than 6 hundredths.
0.4 has 4 tenths and 0.06 has 0 tenths, so 0.4 > 0.06.
8.00 has 8 ones, 0 tenths and 0 hundredths, so it is equal to 8.
0.3 is 30 hundredths, and 30 hundredths is more than 25 hundredths.
5 has 5 ones and 4.99 has only 4 ones, so 5 > 4.99.

questions.prompt: Put these in ascending order (smallest first): 0.3, 0.03, 0.31, 0.1, 0.13
questions.explanation: As hundredths: 3, 10, 13, 30, 31. In ascending order that is 0.03, 0.1, 0.13, 0.3, 0.31.

questions.prompt: Put these in descending order (largest first): 2.5, 2.05, 5.2, 0.25
questions.explanation: 5.2 has 5 ones and 0.25 has 0 ones. 2.5 and 2.05 both have 2 ones, and 5 tenths is more than 0 tenths, so 2.5 > 2.05.
The ones are the same. Then 4 tenths is more than 1 tenth.

questions.prompt: Write 1.5 with two digits after the decimal point, to help compare it with 1.45.
questions.explanation: 5 tenths is the same as 50 hundredths, so 1.5 = 1.50.
